Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: Removing the deferred unlock and placing an explicit unlock only on the success path (line 24) leaves the mutex held when the team is not found. A caller that passes an unknown slug triggers the error return (line 20) while holding the lock, causing a permanent deadlock for the next call to any `Registry` method that acquires the mutex.
Findings.Headline: Mutex left locked on error return — deadlock

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: When `r.Ticket` is nil, the `if` block's body is now empty (just a comment) and execution falls through to `r.Ticket.Key`, which dereferences the nil pointer and panics. The old code returned `r.Body` in that path; the new code removed that return without adjusting the final line. Any caller passing a `Result` with a nil `Ticket` will crash.
Findings.Headline: Nil-pointer dereference when Ticket is nil
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: Changing the condition from `last > len(lines)` to `last >= len(lines)` and setting `last = len(lines) + 1` introduces an off-by-one error. When `last` equals the length of the `lines` slice, the new code sets it to one past the end, causing `lines[first:last]` to panic with an index out-of-range error. This happens, for example, when the hunk ends near the file's end and the requested context lines exactly reach the end.
Findings.Headline: Off-by-one causes slice panic when context reaches file end — blocking

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: The removal of `defer resp.Body.Close()` means the HTTP response body is never closed in any code path. Every successful call to `WhoAmI` will leak an open file descriptor, and under sustained load this will exhaust available descriptors and crash the service. Even on non-2xx status codes or decode errors, the body remains open because the function returns early without closing it.
Findings.Headline: Resource leak: HTTP response body not closed

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: The `depth` field and `pending` slice are shared between goroutines: `Submit` and `Depth` use the mutex, but the worker now writes `depth` and reads `pending` without the lock. A concurrent call to `Depth` while the worker runs `len(q.pending)` is a data race and can return a stale or inconsistent value. Restore the mutex lock/unlock that protected this assignment.
Findings.Headline: Data race on depth field in worker goroutine — blocking

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The `tx.Commit(ctx)` call discards its error value. If the commit fails (e.g., due to a network timeout or deferred constraint violation), the function still returns `nil`, telling the caller the claim was added successfully. Meanwhile, the deferred `tx.Rollback(ctx)` will run, undoing the insert. The caller therefore believes the claim persisted when it did not, leading to silent data loss. The commit error must be checked and propagated.
Findings.Headline: Commit error ignored, silent transaction failure — blocking

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The return values for two error branches are swapped, breaking the contract described in the comment above the function. In the case where `errNoRows` is returned (meaning no claim exists), the function now returns the raw database error instead of the sentinel `ErrNoClaim`. For any other database error, it returns `ErrNoClaim`. Callers checking `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` will now get false positives on database faults and false negatives on a missing claim.
Findings.Headline: Swapped error returns break no-claim vs database-fault contract

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
